summary: No persistent association between an issued ticket and the seat it occupies
description:
Surfaced by the TKT-157 plan draft and made concrete by TKT-161's.

`claim_seats` records which seat identities an inventory claim holds. `tickets` records order, slot and ticket type — **not a seat**. Nothing joins the two, so for any operation that acts on *some* of an order's tickets there is no way to say which seats it acts on.

It bites immediately in the refund path: a **partial** seated refund voids q of Q tickets (TKT-157 picks the lowest ticket ids) but cannot return the corresponding capacity, because no subset of seats can be derived. TKT-161 therefore refuses partial seated *capacity returns* and leaves the obligation visibly outstanding — the refund still completes, so the buyer is repaid and the tickets stop working; only the resale is lost. It will bite TKT-158 (exchange) harder: exchanging one seat of three has the same problem and a worse failure mode.

**Do not solve this inside a refund ticket.** It is a seating-model capability: a ticket occupies a seat, and that fact should be recorded when the ticket is issued.

**Acceptance Criteria:**
- [ ] An issued ticket for a seated claim carries the seat identity it occupies, recorded at issuance rather than derived later.
- [ ] The association survives the seat-identity pinning contract (ADR-029): a seat a sale pins is preserved across published seat-map versions, so the association cannot be invalidated by an ordinary edit.
- [ ] Voiding a subset of an order's tickets identifies exactly the seats to return, and TKT-161's partial-seated refusal can be lifted with a test that proves the right seats came back.
- [ ] Existing seated orders are handled explicitly — backfilled, or documented as unassociated with the consequence stated. Fabricating an association for historical tickets is not acceptable.

Quality gates: `make check` green; contract tests; `organizer_id`-scoped entities.

**Update (TKT-158 planning entry):** the `blocks TKT-158` edge was removed and TKT-158 narrowed to unseated exchanges instead — see TKT-158's `kind=blocker` comment. This ticket remains the prerequisite for **seated** exchange and for lifting TKT-161's partial-seated refusal, both of which are named in their own ACs.

binding.rule: Money is integer minor units + ISO currency code — floats are banned on money paths.

Traceability is a must, for money and tickets: money-relevant records land as immutable, hash-chained, signed journal entries from the first order (corrections = compensating entries; read models = projections), and every ticket/entitlement state change (issued, delivered, transferred, resold, exchanged, redeemed, reissued, invalidated) is an append-only lifecycle event linked to its order.

governingAdrs.why: Every lifecycle event goes through store.appendLifecycle — the verifier asserts one-to-one coverage, so a direct INSERT into lifecycle_events reads as tampering and fails `access verify-lifecycle` in the gate. Canonical forms are pinned by golden literals; changing a byte is a canonical-version migration, not a test update. Also: name the adversary before writing 'tamper-evident'.

Inventory's claim transaction is the contention path. Giving capacity back must go through the same row-locked transaction discipline; a plain UPDATE outside it can drive confirmed_quantity negative or double-return under concurrency.
Capacity adjustments clamp rather than reject. Returning capacity must not let availability exceed the pool's capacity, and the clamp reasoning is the precedent for what to do when it would.

Corrections are COMPENSATING ENTRIES, never mutations. A refund/exchange appends a new signed fact; the original sale fact and its hash link are untouched. The payments journal has a DB trigger that raises on UPDATE/DELETE — any design that 'adjusts' a fact is rejected by the database, not by review.

If any domain event payload changes or a new one is published: bump on CONSUMER SEMANTICS, not parse compatibility, and consumers dispatch on `schema` BEFORE decoding `data`. A fixture built from the type under test cannot fail.

Fail closed. Responses are validated against the spec; an undeclared status code becomes a 500. Every new endpoint must declare every status it can answer, and a downstream answer commerce cannot validate aborts rather than degrades.

Contract-first. A new operation is written in the service's openapi.yaml first, then `openapi_gen.go` / `api-types.gen.ts` are regenerated and COMMITTED before the gate runs — check-generate diffs against HEAD, so an uncommitted regen reads as drift.
Commerce and inventory ARE inside the smoke happy-path coverage gate. A new documented 2xx operation must be exercised through the running stack or the suite fails.

Migrations run out-of-band via each binary's `migrate` subcommand as a one-shot Compose job. Add the SQL under the service's internal/store/migrations/ with the next number; the server path never migrates.

objective.note: Every partial operation on a seated order is currently undefined at the seat level. Refunds under-sell because of it; exchanges would be worse.

scope.note: Whether the association lives on `tickets`, on a join table, or is carried through the issuance event is undecided — it spans inventory (claim_seats), access (tickets) and the ADR-029 pinning contract.

uncertainties.note: Which service owns the association, and how it is established for a claim whose seats are chosen after issuance, if that is even possible.

dependencies.note: Interacts with ADR-029 (seat identity pinning) and ADR-031 (seat-claim pin coordination); belongs with TKT-3/TKT-35.

success.note: Demoable when TKT-161's partial-seated refusal can be lifted and the right seats come back.

context_memo.note: Inherited from TKT-161; ADR-029 and ADR-031 are the constraints, ADR-038 records the refund-side consequence.

comments.body:
<!-- sdlc:stage=backlog kind=readiness -->
### ❌ Implementation readiness — FAIL (deliberately)

The ownership question is genuinely open — the association spans inventory, access and the ADR-029 pinning contract, and no one service obviously owns it. Shaping starts there, not with a plan.

**Note the `blocks TKT-158` edge.** Exchange has the same problem with a worse failure mode: exchanging one seat of three cannot identify which seat leaves. TKT-158's planning must decide whether it restricts itself to unseated exchanges or waits for this.
